en: The Capitals Moved: Choosing Which Sites to Visit
zh: 古都不在同一处：遗址怎么选
ja: 歴代の都は同じ場所ではない：遺跡の選び方

p.src: From the South Gate, the neat rectangle inside the wall can look like the whole of ancient Chang'an. That is the first impression to correct. The wall visible today is chiefly Ming in form. It encloses a later urban core built around the former Tang imperial-city area after contraction at the end of the Tang and subsequent expansion and rebuilding; it is not the Sui-Tang outer city. Fenghao, Qin Xianyang and Han Chang'an lay farther west or north. Xi'an's urban history is not the story of one city repeatedly renamed. Successive capitals were built at different points across the same plain.

p.src: The layered map uses translucent fields to show the capitals' approximate positions relative to one another; it does not pretend to reproduce archaeological boundaries. Feng and Hao lie on opposite banks of the Feng River. Qin Xianyang developed north of the Wei, while its wider palace landscape later crossed the river. Han Chang'an lies northwest of today's wall. Sui Daxing and Tang Chang'an spread far to the east and south. Ming-Qing Xi'an is a much smaller layer within that field. Dashed or generalized edges mark uncertainty or cartographic simplification. Do not use them to locate site entrances.

caption.zh: 历代都城相对位置示意。色块为研究性概化范围，不是考古边界；丰镐两点与秦、汉、隋唐、明清城址不可合并为一座城。
caption.ja: 歴代都城の相対位置を示す模式図。色面は研究用に概略化した範囲で、考古学的境界ではない。豊鎬、秦、漢、隋唐、明清の城址を一つの都市として重ねてはならない。
caption.en: Schematic relative positions of successive capitals. Coloured fields are research generalizations, not archaeological boundaries; Fenghao, Qin, Han, Sui-Tang and Ming-Qing sites must not be merged into one city.

p.src: The earliest capitals lie along the Feng River. Western Zhou Feng stood on the west bank and Hao on the east; together they were not a single regular walled city of the later kind. Written and archaeological evidence commonly treats Hao as the main political centre and associates Feng with ancestral rites, although the detailed site plan remains a subject of research. On the ground, do not search for one complete wall line. Look first at the river, raised ground and the spread of excavated sites. The relationship between the two banks is the essential spatial clue.

p.src: Qin Xianyang was centred on high ground north of the Wei, but the palace and road system built before and after unification was not confined to one walled enclosure. As construction expanded, the palace landscape reached across the river to the south. Tourist maps often place Qin Xianyang, Epang Palace and the First Emperor's mausoleum at Lintong side by side; at a small scale they can look like one attraction. They are separate parts of a broad capital, palace and funerary landscape. Keeping that scale in mind prevents Xianyang Palace, Epang Palace and the Terracotta Army from being mistaken for parts of one site.

p.src: Han Chang'an lies northwest of today's wall. It was not an early version of the Tang grid: palaces, offices and residential areas accumulated through successive building campaigns, producing an irregular plan. Weiyang Palace occupied the southwest part of the Han city. Its protected site covers about 4.84 square kilometres, roughly one seventh of Han Chang'an. That figure describes an entire palace precinct, not one building. At the site, look at the open ground, rammed-earth platforms and surviving routes together. The distances between them convey the scale of the palace precinct.

p.src: Emperor Wen of Sui built a new Daxing City, which the Tang retained and developed as Chang'an. Its order was planned: the palace city stood near the middle of the north side, the imperial city lay immediately south, and the outer city wrapped around them on the east, south and west. Major streets divided wards and markets. Both the Big and Small Wild Goose Pagodas fall within that broad outer-city footprint, while the Ming wall encloses only a smaller northern portion. Walking south on the main axis from the wall toward the pagodas is therefore not leaving Tang Chang'an; it is moving from its government quarter toward wards and temples.

p.src: Daming Palace extended the northern edge of Tang Chang'an onto the higher ground of Longshouyuan. Construction began in 634; after expansion it became the principal seat of government in the mid-seventh century. The palace precinct covered about 3.4 square kilometres, with court, residential and garden zones arranged from south to north. At the heritage park, its scale is clearest in the distances between the platforms, central axis and open spaces. The image below is a contemporary site impression made to communicate that scale. It is neither a historical photograph nor evidence for architectural reconstruction.

caption.zh: 大明宫遗址尺度意象：从开阔地、夯土台基与现代城市远景之间的距离，感受宫城范围。场景用于说明尺度，不作建筑复原。
caption.ja: 大明宮遺跡の尺度を伝える場景。空地、版築基壇、現代都市の遠景の間隔から宮城の広がりを見る。建築復元図ではない。
caption.en: A site-scale study of Daming Palace: open ground, rammed-earth platforms and the distant modern city convey the precinct's extent. It is a study of scale, not an architectural reconstruction.

p.src: Tang Chang'an did not simply shrink evenly. In 904, Han Jian abandoned the badly damaged outer city and palace city, repairing the former imperial city as a new, much smaller Chang'an. That contraction set the broad urban extent from the Five Dynasties through the Yuan. Some Tang roads remained within the reduced city, while inscribed stones left outside were gradually moved in. Present axes such as South Street overlap parts of the Tang imperial-city road system, but this does not mean the whole modern old town preserves the Tang plan. Selected boundaries, routes and institutions endured; the Tang city plan did not survive unchanged.

p.src: In 1369, Fengyuan Circuit became Xi'an Prefecture, establishing Xi'an as the formal city name. During the early Ming expansion, the east and north walls moved outward while the west and south sides were rebuilt along the older city, creating the main outline seen today. The Bell Tower's relocation shows how the city centre shifted. Built in 1384 near the old centre, it became off-centre after expansion and was moved in 1582 to the crossing of the four main streets. Treat that move as the choice of a new centre after Ming expansion; the tower's present position was not the centre of Tang Chang'an.

p.src: Do not try to cover five capitals in one day. For a first sense of the layout, pair the Ming wall and Bell Tower in the morning with either pagoda along the southern axis in the afternoon; this compares the Ming core with the Tang outer city. Give Daming Palace a separate half-day and use its open ground and platforms to grasp palace scale. Han Chang'an and Fenghao are more dispersed, so treat each as its own northwest or western excursion and recheck access and transport before departure. At every site ask four questions: where was the boundary, why was this ground chosen, how did water reach it, and what is archaeological fabric, conservation presentation or later construction?
